title: Svelte and SvelteKit
description: How Svelte compiles components away, what SvelteKit adds, and why runes changed reactivity in Svelte 5.

data.text: Svelte is a compiler, not a runtime. Components are compiled into imperative DOM updates at build time, so the browser loads less framework code than with React or Vue.

data.title: Create a SvelteKit project
data.content: The old `npm create svelte` command was replaced by the `sv` CLI.
data.code:
npx sv create my-app   # choose SvelteKit + TypeScript
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev

rows: Full-stack framework: routing, SSR, form actions
Dev server and bundler used by SvelteKit
Type and accessibility checking for .svelte files

data.caption: src/lib/Counter.svelte — Svelte 5 runes
data.code:
<script lang="ts">
  let count = $state(0);
  let doubled = $derived(count * 2);

  function increment() {
    count += 1;
  }
</script>

<button onclick={increment}>
  {count} (doubled {doubled})
</button>

data.text: Runes (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`) make reactivity explicit and work in plain `.ts` files, not just components. Legacy `export let` props and reactive `$:` statements still work but are no longer the recommended style.

terms.definition: Svelte moves reactivity work to build time instead of shipping a virtual DOM runtime.
The application framework for Svelte: file-based routing, SSR, and server endpoints.
A package that packages the build output for a target platform (node, Vercel, static).
A Svelte 5 compile-time primitive ($state, $derived, $effect) for reactive values.

data.title: What interviewers look for
data.text: Explain that Svelte has no virtual DOM because it compiles updates, and that SvelteKit adds routing, SSR, and form actions on top. Mention runes as the Svelte 5 reactivity model.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Svelte compiles components into efficient DOM updates.
SvelteKit adds routing, SSR, and server load functions.
Runes make reactivity explicit and portable to .ts modules.
data.takeaway: Svelte is the clearest example of a compile-time framework — useful when discussing bundle size and runtime cost.
